newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish prosecutors probe allegations about Walesa.
newsitem.headline: Polish prosecutors probe allegations about Walesa.

text.p: Warsaw prosecutors are probing security service allegations that former President Lech Walesa illegally kept secret documents he should have returned at the end of his term, a spokesman said on Monday.

"We launched an investigation on November 28 into a case regarding a failure to return documents, which a certain person had no right to have at his disposal," said Ryszard Kucinski, spokesman of the Warsaw prosecutors' office.

Walesa, former leader of the Solidarity movement which toppled communism in 1989, firmly denied the allegations, saying they were cooked up by the ruling ex-communists to discredit him before next year's parliamentary elections.

"This is just political fighting. The ex-communists are afraid of the elections...and that is why they are starting to fight early, to hamper actions by people who will soon get at them," Walesa told private Radio Zet from Brussels, where he is on a private visit.

The investigation responds to an official complaint by the State Security Bureau (UOP) that classified documents had leaked from the presidents' office when Walesa was ending his term late last year and that he might have them.
The alleged offences carry a term of up to five years in jail.
Kucinski said the decision on whether to proceed with court action against Walesa or any other person would be taken after two months, time needed to interrogate all the witnesses.
By law, Walesa can only be tried in this case by the State Tribunal, a special court for top state officials, after parliament votes to give the go-ahead.

Walesa, defeated by ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski in presidential elections last year, is trying to unite the splintered right-wing groups against parties rooted in the communist system, in power since 1993.
